utterances.text: In your conclusion you then decide that it's highly probable that it's by Oric.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you exclude the imitation possibility?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: By the examinations following this preliminary conclusion where I compared the construction and proportions of the various elements in these signatures with the corresponding elements in the reference signatures, and I found no differences that might not be accounted for by the natural variation present in anyone's signatures, especially in the signatures I had, the reference signatures I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're referring to the rest of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say: "No differences have been observed which may not be accounted for by natural variation, et cetera." So you found Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. differences?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Just normal variations. Not significant differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you judge normality?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It's based on when you have a number of reference signatures, compare them, and then you can see where the variations are and you can -- by this way you can gain an impression of the width of the variations in the several elements. That's how we compare it. We look at the variations that might be in the questioned signatures fall within the range of the variations which are in the reference samples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a non-probabilistic range, isn't it? Because as you've explained, it's purely approximate in an event.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot quantify the variations, if that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page where you have your conclusions. You conclude: "Highly probable that certain of those signatures were written by the author of the reference signature." You've excluded imitations based on what you've just said. It's not the top level, it's level two.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we established it's the middle level, effectively, of your positive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did not agree with that statement, Mr. Jones. He told you that the first two are definitely very high up. He never conceded that or to accept the use of the word middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can clarify that for us. Very high up, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all conclusions with -- positive conclusions, probably, highly probably, and probability bordering on certainty are all -- I can't say with an exact percentage were all above 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what highly probable means in layman's terms, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean if 10 per cent -- there would be a 10 per cent chance that someone else wrote the signature. There would be 10 out of 100 persons done it and I think this is -- quite a lot of people, still, that might have written the signature. I mean, 10 per cent is still quite a high error rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us at the outset that yours is a nonquantitifiable subject, so is it right for you to be using percentages? It's not right.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I shouldn't attach exactly a number to these conclusions but I just want to say that it must be above 90 per cent, to get an impression of the strength of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event for all of those documents you had a reason for not putting them in the top category, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't set out those reasons in your report, have you?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first place I think this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, the question is: Are they -- is it in your report? Have you stated the reasons why you haven't put those in the top category?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think explicitly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about implicitly?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the annex to the report the strength of the conclusion, that depends on a number of factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you state your reasons implicitly, the reasons set out?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the annex to the report I explained the difference between the probabilities and what the factors are which are influence on this strength.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been good practice in your report to state My doubts are based on the following, and to set those out?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at Q11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Perhaps the witness can tell us in his career how many times or the percentage of times that he's come to the conclusion that a signature is authentic, the highest rate, the highly probable bordering on certainty. How often do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't keep records of this, but I estimate that all the cases with signatures around maybe 40 per cent. But it's an estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's quite common for you to find --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: If we have good quality material and the signature is long enough and complex enough, we might get to this conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The quality, for example, originals, which you had in this case?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at Q11. There you say only probable that it's the same author. So now you're even less sure?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Because this was a copy but it was a better copy than all the other copies I got of the signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Q11 -- a little more doubt and you would be down to probably no not, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. How's that again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. It says possible that Q11 is not Oric's or is not the signature of the purposed author. That has to be right, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: In every case -- and we never give conclusions with certainty. So that means it's always possible that the signature has been made by a person. But the probability that it has been done is very low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll see that. In the next category you say that it's possible --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that Q4, Q7, Q10, and Q16 are by the same author. Now, possible doesn't even appear on your scale normally, doesn't it, on the usual scale that you use?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: On the probability scale, no. It's a separate conclusion we use when you cannot use the probability wordings, as explained in the annex to the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that the copies, maybe if the original was available it would strengthen your conclusion. It could also weaken your conclusion to see the original.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically it could, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say, just looking at -- it's the same page: "The quality of the copies available of the remaining five questioned signatures," and these are the ones we were just looking at, Q4, Q6, Q10, and Q16, "is too poor to allow examination of the writing course and line quality in sufficient detail." In those circumstances wouldn't it be more prudent, more accurate, more scientific, and more professional not to express an opinion at all in that case? Anything is always possible.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: What I could observe is that the signatures have the same design and as far as I -- in whatever I could see on this copy there were no signs of -- there were no deviations or signs, as far as I could judge, of forgery. But that's why I came to no stronger conclusion than possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, it's also possible that it's not the signature?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It sure is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't say that in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's by implication if it's possible that he wrote the signature, then it's also possible that he didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your report, Dr. Fagel. You chose not to say that these documents might possibly be not be Oric's.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't find any indications for forgery in what I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you prepared this report were you being objective or were you simply trying for each specimen to find some way of saying they were that of Oric?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: In every examination I do I always try to look at all possibilities and I take all these possibilities into account when making my observations and making my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you found that every specimen was possibly Oric's. That's what you found?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this copied one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found that in every single specimen at least that it was possibly that of --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Except in one where I had no opinion, Q6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to Q6. Let's come to Q6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if we can actually put Q6 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Q6 is P74 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's P269.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's P74 -- they are both, actually, because I remember yesterday we found out -- when we gave them the number we found out that we also had the same number before. So it's either P74 or 269.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour. So we can have either of the Ps on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 2 of the document where the signature appears. Could we zoom in and enlarge that signature, please. A bit more, maybe. Right. Maybe back a bit. That's good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we can all see that signature. We can see the O, two short lines inside it. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Two short lines in the O?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in the O you can see at the top two lines at the top.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the starting and the ending point of the O?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. There is an O to the left and there are two lines.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think these are separate lines, but they are the start and ending point of the O. If you are looking at the same signature -- but it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may need to look at the K specimens, but -- could we look at -- if I could refer you to your February report, page 2623, or indeed any page, you'll see that the signature characteristically has two lines in the O and then a long horizontal line going through it.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That's for all the other signatures except for this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm coming to that. That's why I was drawing your attention to the two points in there, the two lines. That's the same, isn't it, as the two lines we see in all the other signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's approach it step by step. Let's start with the horizontal line which we see in the K specimens. Now, you've identified that horizontal line as a distinctive feature of the signature, haven't you? It's what's called an element of the signature. I can refer you to your July report page -- the ERN number is 03594722. There you say: "The design of all questioned signatures is similar, the part that can be interpreted as Oric in Cyrillic script, two slash strokes and a long horizontal stroke through these slashes and the rest of the signature." We can see this in all the other signatures -- all the other K signatures. If you give me a moment I'll refer you to the precise page in your February report, for example -- page 03523873. I don't know if everyone has some specimens you can see that long horizontal line. It goes along quite a bit beyond the signature itself. Can you see that if you look at some specimens. Perhaps you could put one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put one on the ELMO. We see it, don't we? A distinctive feature, a big long horizontal line.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It varies, the length of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The length varies, but it's always there. That's pretty important, isn't it? It's an important feature. We'll take it step by step. That's an element.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is one of the most important features.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to your July report.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It's one of the features, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your report and you've picked up on it as one of the most -- one of the distinctive features. "A long horizontal stroke through these slashes"; those are your words.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the features, yes, but not one of the most important features.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, Doctor, you say: "The design of all questioned signatures is similar."

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you refer to a part that can be interpreted to as Oric.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to two slash strokes and then you refer to that line. That's one of the three features that you picked up on yourself.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That's part of the general design, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's precisely the sort of thing you're supposed to be looking for, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the features in the lines which were -- which are curved are more important than straight lines because there's -- these are more difficult to copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you take the reference signatures, do you see a single one where that horizontal line doesn't appear in any of the 35?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they all have the same design as the questioned signatures except for Q6 and I gave an explanation why I think this might be different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a second. It's a question whether it's an important feature or not. Surely, surely, Doctor, if every time I write the name Oric I do a big horizontal line, every single time, and then one time I don't, isn't that the sort of thing you should be looking out for and should note?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I looked for and that's why I tried to give an explanation in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to your explanation. Your explanation, correct if I'm wrong, is that because the name Oric appeared afterwards, it wasn't necessary to put this feature in the O which you saw as being an abbreviation. That's right, isn't it? That's your explanation.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I thought one of the explanations could be in one of the other signatures the name Naser which was written in full in Q6 has been written in short as kind of H which -- represented as the letter N in Cyrillic script --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could have Q6 back on the monitor. You're saying that because Naser was written afterwards, that might be the explanation?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if you can see it, but there are -- the first letter of the name Naser here. Also it seems to have two vertical lines and a horizontal stroke. So it could be -- it's one explanation but I'm not sure -- that this part has been written in the other signatures through the O and the rest of the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the explanation you've come up with.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one that -- a possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that itself a curious feature, that if someone always signs their name with just the surname they had their surname, that's a difference.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I see that people use different versions of their signature, a shorter one and a longer one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he is not suggesting, if I read him well, that he's not agreeing with your proposition that your client only signed his surname. His suggestion is that he signed his surname and over and above and across the two lines plus the line across representing Naser. I mean, that's how I understood him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's a combination of both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. Two questions arising from that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any other signatures that you've seen where the first name also appears in this form?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Not in reference to signatures I had -- I didn't find any signatures and that's why I gave no opinion on this signature because I cannot exclude it on this basis as either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it in your experience odd if I sign my name Jones the whole time and then all of a sudden I'm signing John as well, isn't that feature which you would pick up on and would raise doubt in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I take it into account of course but I say more often in my practice the people use two different signatures, shorter one, sometimes only initials, and a longer one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have two different types of signatures now.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they partly overlap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't your theory based on you concluding that those two lines that appear there are the start and the finish of the O?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, those two lines.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: These lines?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it starts like this and then goes around and then comes back here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take the one on the right, the small one. That's a very deliberate downward slope, isn't it? It's not just someone ending a line.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It fits in with all the other signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell from this copy but it could be a normal line going down from the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to belabour the point, Doctor, but surely those two strokes are the slash strokes in the O which you refer to in your report?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I would need the original to be sure of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even with all those differences, the second type of signature which you hadn't seen before and an O which doesn't have a line through it, even in that case you're not prepared to say that that might not be Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No, because on this base I couldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not conclude that it possibly might not be his, if you're being objective?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: If I could say I can give no opinion, this is one of the possibilities left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday the only reason why you couldn't reach an opinion is because it's a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see it on the ELMO. It looks pretty clear, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we see on the ELMO is fairly clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not clear enough for me to come to an opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it precisely these anomalies that you're supposed to be looking for? These missing lines and --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's also why I look at different possibilities which might explain this, and I gave one of the possibilities in my report. So I couldn't exclude this signature. I mean, I couldn't say that it's probably a forgery or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't prepared to say that that possibly might not be his signature.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I can give no opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. I won't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're not going to pursue it, I won't say anything on it. The paragraph in the report 03523865, that explains the difference between possible, possibly, and no opinion. It explains exactly what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- the points which I put to the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll pass quickly to your July report because -- the same points really, again, you worked from copies and expressed opinions about copies.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Not for all signatures but for some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the same time you said they were too poor to allow examination of the writing course and line quality. I won't put the same point again, but my point is shouldn't you have expressed no opinion?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, I concluded that I couldn't -- as far as I could examine this signature I couldn't find any indications of forgery, but I couldn't see enough detail to come to a positive conclusion. So all I can say is that they are possibly written by the same person who wrote the reference signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except that it might possibly not have been.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That it was implied by implication that it might not have been written by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at a couple of the signatures, and I refer you to -- it's in your report where you set out the signatures. I think it's 03523687 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3867. The previous report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I'm going back to the report to move on to a different point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, your July report, Appendix 2, page 03523867. If we could have that on the ELMO, that would be very helpful. Can we start near the top Q2. The top part. If we can zoom in on Q2. I want to direct your attention, Dr. Fagel, to the dot you see there. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see Q3, that's down and to the left. Again, do you see the dot there at the end?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go down to Q5, please, the dot again do you see it and can you point to it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Q8, again, dot. Clear?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Q20 as well -- sorry, that's two pages over. There it is again, the dot.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've examined the specimen documents, the K documents, and feel free to look at them again. But do any of them have that feature, that dot?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I see in some copies or -- these are not copies, but some dots. But they may be not part of the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the K documents, the specimens.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you see that distinctive dot on any of them, please draw it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. It doesn't appear in any of them, does it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Not in these ones, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that when you did your report?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the things we look at but it's not that important especially we observe often that people sometimes use a dot and sometimes not when they're making signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The difference is this, isn't it, Doctor: When there is a dot the person is finishing with a dot, whereas otherwise they're not. That's the difference, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: People sometimes do finish with the dot and sometimes they don't. For some people -- some people are very consistent in doing so and some people are not. Some of the questioned signatures also don't have a dot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone who signs 35 specimen signatures and doesn't include a single dot is pretty consistent, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they are all made within a short time period, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Doctor, are you trying to find that these signatures are all Oric's or are you considering the possibility that some of these Q6, the ones with the dots, might not be?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I look at the overall results and the missing of dots is one of the results I found, but it's not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't mention it in your report even.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No. We don't explain all similarities and differences in our reports, normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one final question or perhaps series of questions. Looking at your reports you have a reference point. You have: "Suspect: Naser Oric." That's on the Ministry of Justice stationery. I take it he's not a suspect in the Dutch Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's where we put the name of the suspect according to the applicant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It provides you a reference point.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this case, the case of this suspect, have you examined other signatures and other documents in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the case Oric?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- another examination -- I did another examination with signatures in the name of another person. I don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have those names with you?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If not, you can provide it on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This calls for an explanation, at least some kind of explanation now, so at least we know exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can explain, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember the name, something like Dzananovic or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break yesterday at 12.30 p.m. we received from the Prosecution an expert report prepared by this very expert in this very case in which he examined documents in relation to this case and made a finding of probably not the signatures of the purported authors. We're in Rule 68 territory again, as per our motion, as per our request to be informed promptly of this material. This confirmed our suspicion that there are documents in use in this case -- and we're talking about Prosecution exhibits -- which are not authentic. And we wonder how much more of this material is out there and that is why I ask this witness that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I comment, please? Let me first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me just state just for the record that none of us are or were aware of these further examinations and that we are not privy to the documents that you have received, Mr. Jones. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me at least clarify that in my opinion we handed over, and lead counsel can confirm, not during the break but before the start of the testimony of Doctorandus Fagel such report, if he identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid that's not true. I made a note of the time. It was 12.30 p.m., during the break, and Mr. Di Fazio can confirm that. We have the report here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not important and the important thing is there's proper disclosure as far as I am concerned and the relevance and importance of the matter you've just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We simply want to know if there are other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. It's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apart from Dzananovic are there any other?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wubben, we are finished well before the 12.30 deadline that Mr. Jones indicated. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Before I start, we have copies available of the copies we handed over yesterday to Defence counsel. So if you as the Bench want to be provided with those copies, these are available for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please, the usher, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think that unless they are going to be tendered in evidence, we don't need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're not proposing to make this report an exhibit yet. We're proposing to do that during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later on, if we need to see these documents, we'll ask to see them. But for the time being we don't need to bother ourselves with them. Yes, Ms. Sellers, do you need time to consult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May we have a few minutes to consult among ourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I realise that you needed to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. We might get back -- Ms. Patricia Sellers might get back to the documents just referred to later on in re-direct. But I would like first to start to raise some questions with a view to the questions on cross raised and the answering by the expert. Re-examined by Mr. Wubben:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctorandus Fagel, when it comes to the independency of your institute, is it true that on behalf of that independency you're dependant from any instructions or so on from the Dutch government or that Ministry of Justice --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a rather leading question. I wonder if he could be asked to clarify the state of the institute or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a problem of language more than anything else. I'll put the question myself. You describe your institute as enjoying a measure of autonomy, even though it is a part of the Ministry of Justice, a notion with which I am familiar when it comes to the forensic institute in my country as well, and I know exactly why. Could you explain what this autonomy is in the case of your institute and why it is important for the purposes of the work that you conduct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there is no pressures whatsoever on -- to -- any case on the conclusions we have to make. We are free to come to our own conclusion, of course, based on the information that we find in our -- on the exhibits. And of course we only are -- we are, like most government people, subject to the rules of integrity, et cetera. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask: In addition, with a view to these examinations, the first report, the second report, apart from the instructions you confirmed and clarified yesterday and today, did you receive any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. additional instructions from the Dutch government or the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: About this case?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it comes to foreign countries, we have now the Dutch government, but did you receive any instructions or influence, can you comment on that, if so from Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any contact with people from these countries about this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do or were you linked or if so can you comment on any involvement or additional instructions from intelligence agencies during war?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: I had no instructions whatsoever from other agencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In total and in sum, these were the instruction and you felt independent from your professional opinion to judge?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we also at this point need to make aware -- be aware on what were the specific instructions given to him by your office and whether he knew that the instructions were being given not by the Tribunal as such but by the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Perhaps Doctorandus Fagel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware that the instructions came from the Office of the Prosecutor, but I don't know whether it was -- whether the Tribunal itself is aware of this at that moment. I don't know about how you are organised in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to make sure is that you at no time were you given the impression that you were being nominated, appointed, by the Trial Chamber or by the Tribunal itself, that the instructions came and the request came specifically from one branch of this Tribunal, which is, precisely, the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, I knew they -- the instructions came directly from the Office of the Prosecutor, but at that moment -- I don't know whether at that moment also there is some backing from the Tribunal. Because -- actually it doesn't matter too much from my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would it have made a difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. This is the whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for having interrupted you, but again, but I think this was important to clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is all about fact-finding. In addition the last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to the redaction of the report and Mr. Jones referred to this first page and the name of the accused, Naser Oric, and prior to that a "suspect." This word "suspect," do you use that sometimes, always? Can you comment on that. Is this standard or?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It's kind of standard in the Dutch version of our report. This page is modelled to the way we write our Dutch reports and we mention the name of the suspect or victim or whatever the applicant gives us for names, just for reference to be able to recognise what's this case about more easy. We put down these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whenever it's victim or suspect, does that influence your --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: It can be both. The case is brought to us and then there are some administrative data like the numbers, case number, et cetera. We put all these things. If they mention the name of victim, we write down victim such-and-so. If they give us the name of the suspect, we write down the name of the suspect. That's how it works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your professional opinion and practice, there is no influence at all?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it is a suspect or victim, it doesn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So no further questions from the Prosecution. Judge Brydensholt. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. Could the expert witness tell me whether in your experience it has happened to in a case where you have used the criterion "highly probable" or "probable." That it's later shown up that it wasn't true, that there was a falsification? Has that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL [resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it has never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did have some questions for you, but when I heard you say that with regard to those categories you were basically finding yourself in the region of about 90 per cent probability, I am opting not to put the questions; which basically means that we have come to the end of your testimony here, sir. I wish to thank you for the two reports you prepared and the analysis that you carried out. I wish to thank you also for the evidence that you gave in this trial and the way you gave evidence which helped us see through quite a lot of confusion at some time. So I thank you. You will be escorted now out of the courtroom by Madam Usher. And should we encounter any difficulties or you need any assistance on the part of the Tribunal, please draw my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I make one remark, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Someone told me yesterday when I asked for my age I said 45. I don't know if that's true, but it should have been 54. Probably wishful thinking. My apologies. So it's 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Fagel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, you direct me. What time are you expecting that Dr. Koeijer...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He should be here -- sorry. He should be available at 1.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He might be some prior arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could I ask you -- we'll have to break now unless there is any business, other business, that you would like to discuss. But I don't think there is. So we will have a break now. And as soon as we are in a position to resume, possibly before 1.00, will you let us know, someone let us know? Who will be made aware first of the witness's arrival in the Tribunal? Would it be you or the registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, please. It will be the court manager and/or our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the moment -- Mr. Siller, the moment we are more or less -- we know what time we can resume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As soon as we can resume, we'll resume. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break of 30 minutes in any case. Instead of resuming at 1.00 we can resume at 12.30 or quarter to 1.00, it gives us more time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will resume when the witness available which should be not later than 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we bring in the witness. Yes, Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. De Koeijer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence in this case instituted by the Prosecutor against Naser Oric, with which you are familiar already. The practice and the procedure of this Tribunal is that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is being handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. I will explain briefly what the procedure is. I assume you are familiar with courtrooms. Our procedure is similar. You are first going to be asked a series of questions by the lead counsel for the Prosecution, in this case Mr. Wubben, a co-national of yours. And he will be followed by Madam Vidovic who is lead counsel for the accused in this case. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Wubben:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. De Koeijer. To start with can I have your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: It's Jan Adrian de Koeijer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your age?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: I am a document expert working for the Netherlands Forensic Institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Forensic Institute is this?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: The Netherlands Forensic Institute is an institute under the Ministry of Justice and they do work for the police, the prosecuting office, and all other officers which have -- which send in cases. It could be social -- excuse me. It could be financial officers or different types of officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask him if they do work directly for the judicial system, the court system, the courts here in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go into the matter as referred to.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes. We also do work directly for the court system. If the Judge asks us a question we will try to answer that in case work or also if the district attorney or the prosecutor asks us a question we will also try to answer that. We do not work for the other attorneys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that work also include, Dr. De Koeijer, an investigative Judge?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: It can also be for an investigative Judge. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in sum, for the whole judiciary, whenever there is a criminal proceeding in the Netherlands. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long are you employed?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: I have been applied by the NFI from 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are your present duties?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: My present duties is that I am team leader of the documents section. That means I'm responsible for the scientific content of the document section and also for the quality of the case work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you supervise other examiners?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: There are three more other examiners in the document section and I more or less supervise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does supervising mean? Is that only dividing the work or also quality?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: It's quality, R&D, dividing work, but not so much personnel supervision. I don't have any authority over them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're a supervisor over other document examiners.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: I've been that for -- since 19 -- well, 1996, roughly, I think, since the time that I became a certified document examiner myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me about the formal education. What education as a background do you have?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: By background is in chemistry. I did the university degree in chemistry, a Master's degree at the University of Utrecht.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry the Master's degree, that's referring to the title of doctorandus?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Doctorandus, yes. It's similar to a Master's. That was analytical chemistry that I studied. Then I had other employment and then I came to the NFI. And then I was trained on the job as a document examiner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain more about this other training?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: The training on the job means that I have a mentor and he trains me in the business of documents while doing case work. This training went on for a period of four years where I learned to do case work. I also did some other courses like a printing course at a printing school. I've done also some internal courses on reporting on law and some -- well, some others I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me: How many cases do you examine on -- in a given year?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Per year, our document section does roughly between 150 and 200 cases at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which you supervise?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Which I supervise. I check every case before it goes out of the laboratory. I do not do all these cases myself. I -- on average, the last few years I would probably do about 15 cases a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these analysis, these document examinations, these form -- and the supervising -- form the regular part of your duty?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some background about memberships of colleagues, fellows national or international, if applicable of course.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: I am at the moment the chairman of the European Documents Working Group. That is a group of document experts of which 35 or 40 countries are now a member within Europe. I am chairman of the steering committee of that group. I have been a member of this committee for almost a bit more than six years now and previously been chairman also for two years before that. I am a member of the America Academy of Forensic Science and the America Society of Questioned Document Examiners. And I am also a member of the steering committee of the Netherlands Quality Circle for Documents and Currency. That's an internal group within the Netherlands where all document experts will meet on a regular basis and I am a member of that steering committee after being chairman of that steering committee for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to a quality circle like that, is it only national or does your laboratory also maintain international --

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: This quality circle is national, but the European Document Experts Working Group is international, it's European. And we also have some liaison with some similar group in the United States and in Australia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you update each other through e-mail of the latest findings or is it something like to --

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: We have meetings. Once every two years there is a European conference which we organise and twice every year the steering committee will meet and discuss matters concerning document examination like Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. harmonisation of methods and procedures within the document world, training, quality-assurance issues. Those kind of things we discuss within the steering committee and we also try to implement them European-wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I move to the issues of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'll try to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will move now to the issue of publications from your hand. Can you confirm, clarify, your publications on forensic documents from the past years, from what time on.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: I have co-authored a number of different publications on the analysis of inks on documents. I have also done a number of lectures at conferences on ink analysis and other -- some technical aspects of document examination. These papers have also then been written down in the proceedings of these conferences. I'm not sure how much more -- you want me to state each paper separately?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not each paper separately, but what is important on what variety of specialism as far as applicable to the report you made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic, do you have any problems with the qualifications of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suggest to you that you move to more substantive matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: First -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next issue will be -- my question, if you can give to the Judges as a general introduction what kind of method your laboratory, your institute, uses for document examination and then focus on stamp impressions and document tampering.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: We have a number of different methods which we generally apply to these kind of questions. If I first start with examination of stamps. Mainly this is done -- if it is a stamp comparison, we will usually overlay two different stamps. That can be done either digitally by scanning them in and using image analysis packages or manually by copying them on a transfer sheet. In this case, we did it digitally. Also, we will do microscopical examinations of the stamps to look for small detail in the stamp which is repetitive in the stamps. We will look often, if asked, at the ink of the stamps to see if the ink is the same of the different stamps; we did not do this in this case. Furthermore, we -- for stamp examination, we will first of all of course see if it is a real stamp or not. If the impression is made by a rubber stamp or if it is, for example, a printed forgery. That is of course one of the first examinations that takes place. For looking for tampering on documents, we will use different methods. One is looking for mechanical erasures. We can do this using electrostatic devices, which we use for impression work. We can do this from transparent lighting, lighting coming from beneath the document, or by using side lighting which shows more relief in the document. We will use different luminescent techniques, techniques like ultraviolet or infrared luminescence, to detect possible latent pieces of ink which are not visible to the naked eye but which may be visible under luminescent light. This may also show us if the document has been stained chemically by, for example, inks fading into the document using chemicals. utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: We only used nondestructive examination techniques to examine these documents. First of all, the documents are usually examined for indented writing impressions using the electrostatic detection device. Afterwards we examined the documents microscopically to see if there are any specific areas which we need to address further using other techniques. We scanned in the documents, specifically the stamp area, and isolated the stamps and afterwards superimposed the stamps one on top of each on the screen to see if they match, the image matches. Furthermore, we examined the stamps microscopically to see if the minute -- well, we call them damages to the rim of the stamp, were consistent in the different stamps we examined. We also determined microscopically if we were dealing with an original document or with a photocopied document. And we examined them using fluorescence to see if any chemical erasure had taken place or any latent ink was present that couldn't be seen with the naked eye.

Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER

If the signature is a genuine signature; that means if it's not a printed signature by ink-jet printer or laser printer, or if it's not been traced, if there are no lines from tracing visible. Other areas are, for example, the stamp just to see if it's an original stamp or not. Also, the whole document in general is examined for erasure, mechanical erasure or chemical erasure. Because we do not understand the language of these documents, it was difficult to identify specific areas on the basis of content which we should address for thoroughly for this work, so we took the document as a whole and examined it as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does an "examination for indented writing" include?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Examination for indented writing is done by an instrument called the electrostatic detection apparatus. It is an instrument where the document is placed on a vacuum board and hence -- after that a piece of plastic foil is pulled over the document. It is then electrostatically charged, the combination of document and foil. After the charge has settled we apply toner and this toner will build up in the areas where there are indentations on the document. So if there are indentations from previous writing on the document, then there the toner will build up and give us like almost a photocopy image of the indentations of the -- which are present on the document. But it will also give us an image of any other disturbance of the paper fibres on the surface. So it will show if there has been any mechanical erasure on this document because then you will have paper fibre disturbances, which will be clearly visible on the sheet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also clarify this so-called infrared luminescence examination.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: Infrared luminescence is a very frequently used technique in document examination. What happens is we have a document, we shine a very bright light on to it, that could be light of different colours, blue to red. What happens then is the ink will absorb this light and send out light of a different wavelength. We call this luminescence or fluorescence. This light will be captured by a camera and we can see the ink light up under this light. Because different inks behave in different ways under this luminescence work, we can see, for example, if there are different inks on this one document. Sometimes it is so that if an ink is erased from a document or entry, that still there are components remaining in the paper which will show this fluorescence but it will not be visible to the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

We call these a quire . The war diary consisted of a total of five quires. What we saw is the number of pages per quire, they differed quite amazingly.

utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Sorry again to interrupt you, but I think we need to clear this. You said: Similarity of index 0 means we cannot find any real similarity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually in the explanation that you have on the -- in your report, 0 does not mean that you haven't been able to find any real similarity but it says: "No conclusion possible due to insufficient quality of the stamp impression." I think the two explanations are not the same, so perhaps you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. The latter is correct. What is underneath the table is the correct explanation. 0 means the stamp quality is so poor that even though we find similarities, it's not possible to draw a conclusion on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 1, to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: 1 is we have a limited number of features visible and often in combination with the poor quality of the stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 2?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: 2 is a reasonable amount of features and usually also a reasonable stamp quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now I turn again to Appendix 4 of your report called Features in Stamp Impression on that specific document, and we already addressed that one. And you as an expert gave your opinion on this stamp. Now when we know what's in the table, table 1 -- you earlier described in the various columns -- how does table 1 apply to this stamp impression on document 02075808?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: From table 1 we can see that it was an original typewritten document. This is also an original stamp impression. It is of reasonable quality and we see four of these highlighted features present. The combination of reasonable quality and four highlighted features gives us a similarity index of two, which is a measure for the conclusion we will be drawing later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 2 is, I take it, is that a top score or a middle score?

utterances.speaker: JAN ADRIAAN de KOEIJER
utterances.text: That is for us the top score. If the quality was -- had been so good that you could see all the details in the stamp, there may have been higher numbers. But in this case with this quality of stamps, this is the highest we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, as a subsequent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got three more minutes. So.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My subsequent issue will take more than four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can stop here. Dr. De Koeijer, I suppose it has been explained to you already that you will need to return tomorrow to continue and finish with your testimony. So please God we will adjourn. We will meet tomorrow morning in the same courtroom at 9.00. I thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
